danish.title: Ottende bog (1811–12) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Næste dag tog grev Rostov på Marja Dmitrijevnas råd Natasja med på besøg hos fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskij. Greven begav sig ikke muntert af sted på dette besøg; i sit hjerte var han bange. Han huskede tydeligt det sidste møde, han havde haft med den gamle fyrste på rekrutteringstidspunktet, hvor han som svar på en invitation til middag havde måttet lytte til en vred irettesættelse for ikke at have stillet sin fulde kvote af mænd. Natasja, der derimod havde taget sin bedste kjole på, var i det allerbedste humør. »De kan ikke lade være med at holde af mig,« tænkte hun. »Alle har altid holdt af mig, og jeg er så villig til at gøre alt, hvad de ønsker, så parat til at holde af ham — fordi han er hans far — og af hende — fordi hun er hans søster — at der ingen grund er til, at de ikke skulle holde af mig...«
De kørte op til det dystre gamle hus på Vozdvizjenka og gik ind i forhallen.

»Nå, Vorherre være os nådig!« sagde greven, halvt i spøg, halvt i alvor; men Natasja lagde mærke til, at hendes far var befippet, da han trådte ind i forværelset, og spagfærdigt og sagte spurgte, om fyrsten og fyrstinden var hjemme.

Da de var blevet anmeldt, opstod der tydelig uro blandt tjenestefolkene. Tjeneren, der var gået ind for at melde dem, blev standset af en anden i den store hal, og de hviskede til hinanden. Så løb en stuepige ind i hallen og sagde hastigt noget, idet hun nævnte fyrstinden. Til sidst kom en gammel, gretten tjener og meddelte Rostoverne, at fyrsten ikke modtog, men at fyrstinden bad dem gå op. Den første person, der kom de besøgende i møde, var mademoiselle Bourienne. Hun hilste far og datter med særlig høflighed og fulgte dem til fyrstindens værelse. Fyrstinden, der så ophidset og nervøs ud med røde pletter i ansigtet, kom løbende de besøgende i møde med tunge skridt og forgæves forsøg på at virke hjertelig og afslappet. Fra første øjekast brød fyrstinde Marja sig ikke om Natasja. Hun syntes, hun var for moderigtigt klædt, letsindig munter og forfængelig. Hun var slet ikke klar over, at hun, før hun havde set sin kommende svigerinde, var forudindtaget imod hende af ufrivillig misundelse på hendes skønhed, ungdom og lykke, samt af jalousi over broderens kærlighed til hende. Udover denne uovervindelige antipati var fyrstinde Marja netop da oprørt, fordi den gamle fyrste, da Rostoverne blev anmeldt, havde skreget, at han ikke ønskede at se dem, at fyrstinde Marja kunne gøre det, hvis hun ville, men at de ikke måtte lukkes ind til ham. Hun havde besluttet at modtage dem, men frygtede, at fyrsten hvert øjeblik kunne finde på et eller andet udfald, da han syntes meget opbragt over Rostovernes besøg.

»Nå, kære fyrstinde, her har jeg bragt min sangerinde,« sagde greven, idet han bukkede og så sig uroligt om, som bange for at den gamle fyrste kunne dukke op. »Jeg er så glad for, at I kan lære hinanden at kende... meget ked af, at fyrsten stadig er svagelig,« og efter et par flere almindelige bemærkninger rejste han sig. »Hvis De tillader, at jeg overlader min Natasja til Dem for et kvarters tid, fyrstinde, kører jeg lige et smut hen og besøger Anna Semjonovna, det er lige i nærheden på Hundepladsen, og så henter jeg hende bagefter.«

Greven havde udtænkt denne diplomatiske finte (som han bagefter fortalte sin datter) for at give de kommende svigerinder lejlighed til at tale frit med hinanden, men et andet motiv var at undgå faren ved at møde den gamle fyrste, som han frygtede. Han nævnte det ikke for sin datter, men Natasja bemærkede sin fars nervøsitet og uro og følte sig ydmyget over det. Hun rødmede for ham, blev endnu mere vred over at rødme, og så på fyrstinden med et dristigt og trodsigt udtryk, der sagde, at hun ikke var bange for nogen. Fyrstinden fortalte greven, at hun ville være henrykt, og bad ham blot om at blive lidt længere hos Anna Semjonovna, og han gik.

Trods de urolige blikke, fyrstinde Marja sendte hende — idet hun ønskede at tale under fire øjne med Natasja — blev mademoiselle Bourienne siddende i stuen og talte vedholdende om Moskvas forlystelser og teatre. Natasja følte sig krænket over den tøven, hun havde bemærket i forværelset, over sin fars nervøsitet og over fyrstindens unaturlige optræden, der — mente hun — gjorde hende en nåde ved at modtage hende, og derfor mishagede alt hende. Hun brød sig ikke om fyrstinde Marja, som hun syntes var meget kedelig, affekteret og tør. Natasja trak sig pludselig ind i sig selv og antog ufrivilligt en nedladende mine, der fjernede fyrstinde Marja endnu mere. Efter fem minutters pinlig, tvungen samtale hørte de lyden af tøffelklædte fødder, der hastigt nærmede sig. Fyrstinde Marja så forskrækket ud.
Døren gik op, og den gamle fyrste i morgenkappe og hvid natkappe kom ind.

»Ah, frue!« begyndte han. »Frue, grevinde... grevinde Rostova, hvis jeg ikke tager fejl... Jeg beder Dem undskylde, undskylde mig... Jeg vidste det ikke, frue. Gud er mit vidne, jeg vidste ikke, at De havde beæret os med et besøg, og jeg kom ind i dette kostume kun for at se min datter. Jeg beder Dem undskylde... Gud er mit vidne, det vidste jeg ikke —« gentog han og lagde unaturligt og ubehageligt tryk på ordet »Gud«, så fyrstinde Marja stod med sænkede øjne og ikke turde se hverken på sin far eller på Natasja.
Heller ikke sidstnævnte, der var rejst og havde nejet, vidste hvad hun skulle gøre. Kun mademoiselle Bourienne smilede venligt.
»Jeg beder Dem undskylde, undskylde mig! Gud er mit vidne, det vidste jeg ikke,« mumlede den gamle mand, og efter at have betragtet Natasja fra top til tå gik han ud.

Mademoiselle Bourienne var den første, der fattede sig efter dette syn, og begyndte at tale om fyrstens upasselighed. Natasja og fyrstinde Marja så på hinanden i tavshed, og jo længere de gjorde det uden at sige, hvad de ville sige, desto større blev deres antipati mod hinanden.

Da greven vendte tilbage, var Natasja uhøfligt lettet og skyndte sig med at komme af sted: i det øjeblik hadede hun den stive, ældre fyrstinde, der kunne bringe hende i en så pinlig situation og havde tilbragt en halv time med hende uden én gang at nævne fyrst Andrej. »Jeg kunne ikke begynde at tale om ham i den franske kvindes nærværelse,« tænkte Natasja. Den samme tanke plagede imens fyrstinde Marja. Hun vidste, hvad hun burde have sagt til Natasja, men hun havde ikke kunnet sige det, fordi mademoiselle Bourienne var i vejen, og fordi hun, uden at vide hvorfor, følte det meget vanskeligt at tale om ægteskabet. Da greven allerede var på vej ud af stuen, gik fyrstinde Marja hastigt hen til Natasja, tog hendes hånd og sagde med et dybt suk:
»Vent, jeg må...«
Natasja kiggede ironisk på hende uden at vide hvorfor.
»Kære Natalie,« sagde fyrstinde Marja, »jeg vil have dig at vide, at jeg er glad for, at min bror har fundet lykken...«
Hun standsede, da hun følte, at hun ikke talte sandt. Natasja lagde mærke til det og gættede årsagen.
»Jeg synes, fyrstinde, at det ikke er belejligt at tale om det nu,« sagde hun med ydre værdighed og kulde, selvom hun mærkede, at tårerne kvalte hende.
»Hvad har jeg sagt, og hvad har jeg gjort?« tænkte hun, så snart hun var ude af stuen.
De ventede længe på, at Natasja skulle komme til middag den dag. Hun sad på sit værelse og græd som et barn, snød næse og hulkede. Sonja stod ved siden af hende og kyssede hendes hår.
»Natasja, hvad drejer det sig om?« spurgte hun. »Hvad rager de dig? Det går alt sammen over, Natasja.«
»Men hvis du bare vidste, hvor krænkende det var... som om jeg...«
»Tal ikke om det, Natasja. Det var ikke din skyld, så hvorfor tage det tungt? Giv mig et kys,« sagde Sonja.
Natasja løftede hovedet, kyssede sin veninde på læberne og trykkede sit våde ansigt mod hendes.
»Jeg kan ikke forklare det, jeg ved det ikke. Ingen har skyld,« sagde Natasja — »Det er min skyld. Men det gør alt sammen så forfærdelig ondt. Åh, hvorfor kommer han ikke?...«

Hun kom til middag med røde øjne. Marja Dmitrijevna, der vidste, hvordan fyrsten havde modtaget Rostoverne, lod som om hun ikke bemærkede, hvor ked af det Natasja var, og spøgte resolut og højlydt ved bordet med greven og de andre gæster.

english.title: Book Eight (1811 - 12) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: The next day, on Marya Dmitrievna's advice, Count Rostov took Natasha to call on Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky. The count did not set out cheerfully on this visit — at heart he was afraid. He clearly remembered his last meeting with the old prince at the time of the enrollment, when in reply to a dinner invitation he had been forced to listen to an angry scolding for not having provided his full quota of men. Natasha, on the other hand, having put on her best dress, was in the highest spirits. "They can't help liking me," she thought. "Everybody always has liked me, and I'm so willing to do anything they want, so ready to be fond of him — for being his father — and of her — for being his sister — that there's no reason for them not to like me..."
They drove up to the gloomy old house on the Vozdvizhenka and entered the vestibule.

"Well, the Lord have mercy on us!" said the count, half joking, half serious; but Natasha noticed that her father was flustered on entering the anteroom and inquired timidly and softly whether the prince and princess were at home.

When they had been announced, a commotion was noticeable among the servants. The footman who had gone to announce them was stopped by another in the large hall and they whispered to each other. Then a maid ran into the hall and hurriedly said something, mentioning the princess. At last an old, cross-looking footman came and announced to the Rostovs that the prince was not receiving, but that the princess asked them to come up. The first person to meet the visitors was Mademoiselle Bourienne. She greeted father and daughter with special politeness and showed them to the princess's room. The princess, looking excited and nervous, her face flushed in patches, ran in to meet the visitors, treading heavily, and trying in vain to appear warm and at ease. From the first glance, Princess Mary did not like Natasha. She thought her too fashionably dressed, frivolously gay, and vain. She didn't at all realize that before having seen her future sister-in-law she was already prejudiced against her by involuntary envy of her beauty, youth, and happiness, as well as by jealousy of her brother's love for her. Apart from this unconquerable dislike, Princess Mary was agitated just then because when the Rostovs were announced, the old prince had shouted that he did not wish to see them, that Princess Mary might do so if she chose, but they were not to be admitted to him. She had decided to receive them, but feared the prince might do something unpredictable at any moment, as he seemed very upset by the Rostovs' visit.

"There, my dear princess, I've brought you my songbird," said the count, bowing and looking around uneasily as if afraid the old prince might appear. "I'm so glad you should get to know each other... very sorry the prince is still unwell," and after a few more commonplace remarks he rose. "If you'll allow me to leave my Natasha in your care for a quarter of an hour, Princess, I'll drive around to see Anna Semenovna — it's quite near, in Dogs' Square — and then I'll come back for her."

The count had devised this diplomatic move (as he later told his daughter) to give the future sisters-in-law a chance to talk freely, but another motive was to avoid the danger of meeting the old prince, of whom he was afraid. He didn't mention this to his daughter, but Natasha noticed her father's nervousness and anxiety and felt embarrassed by it. She blushed for him, grew still angrier at having blushed, and looked at the princess with a bold and defiant expression that said she wasn't afraid of anybody. The princess told the count she would be delighted, and only asked him to stay longer at Anna Semenovna's, and he left.

Despite the uneasy glances thrown at her by Princess Mary — who wanted to have a private talk with Natasha — Mademoiselle Bourienne remained in the room and kept chattering about Moscow amusements and theaters. Natasha felt offended by the hesitation she had noticed in the anteroom, by her father's nervousness, and by the princess's unnatural manner — which she felt was a matter of doing her a favor by receiving her — and so everything displeased her. She didn't like Princess Mary, whom she thought very plain, affected, and stiff. Natasha suddenly drew into herself and involuntarily assumed a standoffish air that alienated Princess Mary still further. After five minutes of awkward, strained conversation, they heard the sound of slippered feet approaching rapidly. Princess Mary looked frightened.
The door opened and the old prince, in a dressing gown and a white nightcap, came in.

"Ah, madam!" he began. "Madam, Countess... Countess Rostova, if I'm not mistaken... I beg you to excuse me, to excuse me... I had no idea, madam. God is my witness, I didn't know you had honored us with a visit, and I came in this state only to see my daughter. I beg you to excuse me... God is my witness, I didn't know—" he repeated, stressing the word "God" so unnaturally and so unpleasantly that Princess Mary stood with her eyes lowered, not daring to look at either her father or Natasha.
Natasha, having risen and curtsied, didn't know what to do either. Mademoiselle Bourienne alone smiled pleasantly.
"I beg you to excuse me, excuse me! God is my witness, I didn't know," muttered the old man, and after looking Natasha over from head to foot he went out.

Mademoiselle Bourienne was the first to recover after this apparition and began talking about the prince's illness. Natasha and Princess Mary looked at each other in silence, and the longer they looked without saying what they wanted to say, the greater their dislike of each other grew.

When the count returned, Natasha was impolitely eager to leave. At that moment she hated the stiff, elderly princess who could place her in such an embarrassing position and had spent half an hour with her without once mentioning Prince Andrew. "I couldn't start talking about him in front of that Frenchwoman," thought Natasha. The same thought was meanwhile tormenting Princess Mary. She knew what she ought to have said to Natasha, but she had been unable to say it because Mademoiselle Bourienne was in the way, and because, without knowing why, she found it very hard to speak about the marriage. When the count was already leaving the room, Princess Mary went up quickly to Natasha, took her by the hand, and said with a deep sigh:
"Wait, I must..."
Natasha glanced at her sarcastically without knowing why.
"Dear Natalie," said Princess Mary, "I want you to know that I'm glad my brother has found happiness..."
She paused, feeling that she was not telling the truth. Natasha noticed this and guessed its reason.
"I think, Princess, it is not the right time to speak of that now," she said with outward dignity and coldness, though she felt tears choking her.
"What have I said and what have I done?" she thought, as soon as she was out of the room.
They waited a long time for Natasha to come to dinner that day. She sat in her room crying like a child, blowing her nose and sobbing. Sonya stood beside her, kissing her hair.
"Natasha, what is it about?" she asked. "What do they matter to you? It will all pass, Natasha."
"But if you only knew how offensive it was... as if I..."
"Don't talk about it, Natasha. It wasn't your fault, so why should you mind? Kiss me," said Sonya.
Natasha raised her head and, kissing her friend on the lips, pressed her wet face against hers.
"I can't explain, I don't know. No one's to blame," said Natasha. "It's my fault. But it all hurts terribly. Oh, why doesn't he come?..."

She came in to dinner with red eyes. Marya Dmitrievna, who knew how the prince had received the Rostovs, pretended not to notice how upset Natasha was and joked cheerfully and loudly at table with the count and the other guests.
